name: Calculus
title: Calculus intuition
intro: Calculus studies change and accumulation. Limits make precise what happens as you zoom in; derivatives measure instantaneous rate of change; integrals add up infinitely many small pieces. These lessons build intuition and the core rules — product, chain, and the Fundamental Theorem — with simple techniques for everyday problems. Algebra fluency with functions and graphs is assumed.

lessons.title: Limits intuition
lessons.summary: What value a function approaches as the input approaches a point.

sections.p: The limit lim<sub>x→a</sub> f(x) = L means: as x gets arbitrarily close to a (from either side, in the two-sided limit), f(x) gets arbitrarily close to L. The function need not equal L at a — or even be defined there.
f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1) is undefined at x = 1, but for x ≠ 1 it equals x + 1. So lim<sub>x→1</sub> f(x) = 2.
Left-hand lim<sub>x→a−</sub> and right-hand lim<sub>x→a+</sub> may differ (jump). The two-sided limit exists only when both exist and agree.

lim<sub>x→∞</sub> 1/x = 0: values approach 0 as x grows without bound. Vertical asymptotes often mean a limit is infinite (grows without bound), which is a useful description even though ∞ is not a real number.

lessons.title: The derivative idea
lessons.summary: Instantaneous rate of change as a limit of slopes.

sections.p: Average rate of change of f from a to a+h is [f(a+h) − f(a)] / h — the slope of a secant. The derivative f′(a) is the limit of that quotient as h → 0: slope of the tangent line, when the limit exists.
For f(x) = x² at a = 3: [ (3+h)² − 9 ] / h = [9 + 6h + h² − 9]/h = 6 + h → 6. So f′(3) = 6. In general (x²)′ = 2x.
If f is position (meters) and x is time (seconds), f′ is velocity (m/s). If f is cost and x is items, f′ is marginal cost.

lessons.title: Basic differentiation rules
lessons.summary: Power, constant, sum and constant-multiple rules.

sections.p: Once you trust the limit definition, shortcuts save time. These rules hold on intervals where the functions are differentiable.

sections.p: (eˣ)′ = eˣ. (ln x)′ = 1/x for x > 0. These are the natural pair for growth and accumulation.
Products and nested functions need their own rules. The product rule is not “derivative of each times each” alone — there is a cross of terms.

lessons.title: Applications of derivatives
lessons.summary: Tangents, motion, related rates sketch and max/min.

sections.p: Derivatives answer “how fast?” and “which way is the graph bending?” They also locate candidates for maximum and minimum values.
At x = a, slope m = f′(a); line: y − f(a) = m(x − a).
Where f′(x) = 0 or f′ is undefined (in the domain). First or second derivative tests classify local max/min. Endpoints matter on a closed interval.
Position s(t); velocity v = s′; acceleration a = v′ = s″. Speed is |v|.
Express the quantity to optimize as a function of one variable, find critical points, compare values. Example: maximize area for fixed fence length.

lessons.title: Integrals as area
lessons.summary: Riemann sums and the definite integral as net signed area.

sections.p: To approximate the area under y = f(x) from x = a to x = b, slice [a,b] into n strips, form rectangles of height f(at a sample point) and width Δx, and add. As n → ∞ and Δx → 0, the sum approaches the definite integral ∫ab f(x) dx when f is nice enough.
Above the x-axis contributes positively; below, negatively. Net integral can be zero even when geometric area is not.

sections.p: Under y = 1 from 0 to 2: area 2. Under y = x from 0 to 2: triangle area (1/2)×2×2 = 2. Under y = x² the exact value needs antiderivatives (next lessons).

lessons.title: Fundamental Theorem intuition
lessons.summary: Derivatives and integrals undo each other.

sections.p: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (FTC) links the two halves of calculus. If F′ = f, then ∫ab f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a). Accumulation from a to b is the net change of an antiderivative.
F is an antiderivative of f when F′ = f. Antiderivatives differ by a constant: if F works, so does F + C.
d/dx ∫<sub>a</sub><sup>x</sup> f(t) dt = f(x) (for continuous f). The derivative of “area so far” recovers the height.
∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C denotes the family of antiderivatives. The +C matters until limits fix the constant.

lessons.title: Simple integration techniques
lessons.summary: Power rule reverse, substitution hint and splitting sums.

sections.p: Many integrals reduce to reversing differentiation rules. Start with linearity and the power rule; use substitution when a chain-rule pattern appears.

sections.code:
∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + C   (n ≠ −1)
∫ x⁻¹ dx = ln|x| + C
∫ eˣ dx = eˣ + C

sections.p: ∫ (af + bg) = a∫f + b∫g. Split sums and pull out constants before integrating term by term.
If you see f′(g(x)) g′(x), set u = g(x), du = g′(x) dx. Example: ∫ 2x cos(x²) dx; u = x², du = 2x dx → ∫ cos u du = sin(x²) + C.
